opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the thing people underestimate is how tight the tolerances are in a lot of manufacturing. If you're doing assembly, inserting a pin into a hole, seating a connector, routing a cable, you're often talking about fractions of a millimeter. And traditional industrial robots get there by being extremely stiff, extremely repeatable machines. They don't really "know" where anything is; they just go to the exact same joint positions every single time, and the whole cell is engineered around that: fixtures, jigs, parts presented in exactly the same place.

The promise of AI-controlled robots is that you can throw away a lot of that rigid engineering and have the robot perceive and adapt. But learned policies today are kind of fuzzy. They're great at the gross motion, getting roughly to the right place, handling variation in where an object is sitting, but the last few millimeters is where they struggle. You've got noise in the camera estimates, calibration drift, the policy itself has some variance, and those errors all stack up. A model that's 95% successful at grabbing a cup is amazing for a demo, but in a factory a 95% success rate on one step is a disaster, because you've got dozens of steps and the line has to run all day.

There's also a feedback problem. Humans do precise work mostly through touch, not vision. You feel the peg catch the edge of the hole and you wiggle it in. Most of the current robot learning stacks are very vision-heavy, and vision just isn't the right sensor for the final contact-rich part of the task. Until you get good force and tactile feedback integrated into these policies, and the reliability to match, it's hard to justify replacing a dumb but perfectly repeatable machine with a smart but occasionally wrong one.

So I think the near-term opportunity is a hybrid: let the AI handle the parts that need flexibility and perception, and lean on classical precision mechanics, compliance, and clever fixturing for the parts that need tight tolerances. Over time, as the models get better at contact and the reliability numbers climb into the "four nines" range, that boundary moves. But right now precision and reliability are really the gap between a cool research video and something a plant manager will actually put on their line.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I ran into really directly at Cobalt, and it's kind of the dirty secret of applying modern AI to robotics. When you look at what manufacturing robots actually do today, the bar is incredibly high. A robot arm on an automotive line is placing a weld or inserting a part with sub-millimeter repeatability, and it's doing that thousands of times a day with essentially zero failures. That's the baseline, and it's been that way for decades because you solve it with classical control: you know exactly where the robot is, you know exactly where the part is, and you program the trajectory.

The problem is that learned systems, the end-to-end neural policies that everyone's excited about, are great at the stuff classical robotics is terrible at. Generalization, dealing with clutter, handling an object it's never seen before. But they tend to be sloppy. A vision-language-action model might get the grasp right ninety-five percent of the time, and it'll be off by a centimeter here and there. In a home or a demo video, that's fine, you just try again. On a production line, a ninety-five percent success rate is a disaster. If you're assembling ten thousand units a day and five hundred of them have a misaligned part, you've just shut down the plant.

So there's this mismatch. Manufacturing is actually the environment where you least need the flexibility that AI gives you, because everything is already structured and repeatable, and it's the environment where you most need the precision that AI is worst at. The economics push you toward the boring solution. Why would I replace a fixture and a programmed trajectory that works perfectly with a model that's probabilistic?

Where I think it gets interesting is the hybrid approach. You use the learned model for perception and high-level decisions, figuring out what to do and roughly where things are, and then you hand off to a classical controller for the last few millimeters. That's where I've seen things actually work. And honestly, I think the first real wins for AI in robotics are going to come from places that look less like a factory and more like a warehouse or a hospital hallway, where the tolerance for a bit of imprecision is much higher and the value is in handling the long tail of weird situations.

r001.rationale: The response says a 95% grasp success rate is a disaster and describes sub-millimeter repeatability for automotive weld placement, but it does not state that 99% positioning accuracy is insufficient.

astra-6.text:
The challenge is that manufacturing often requires much more precision than simply getting an object roughly into the right place. If you’re inserting a connector, being a little off can mean it doesn’t go in, or you damage the part. And you need that to work reliably over thousands of repetitions.

Traditional automation gets that precision by controlling the environment: you have fixtures that hold everything in exactly the same position, and the robot repeats a very specific motion. Once you ask an AI-controlled robot to handle variation, it has to perceive those small differences and correct for them, often using force or touch as well as vision. So understanding what to do is only part of the problem. Executing it with the accuracy and consistency a production line needs is a separate challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge is that a lot of manufacturing tasks require much more precision than something like picking an object up off a table. If you’re inserting a connector or fitting two parts together, being a millimeter off can mean it doesn’t work at all. And you need to do that reliably, thousands of times in a row.

Traditional automation gets that precision by controlling the environment: you build fixtures that hold every part in exactly the right place, and the robot repeats a carefully programmed motion. AI offers the possibility of handling more variation, but recognizing what needs to happen isn’t the same as executing it precisely. You need perception, motion control, and often force feedback working together to make those last little adjustments. That’s a much harder problem than producing a motion that looks roughly right.
